To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The brain regions that are active when people draw simple conclusions from linguistic material (elementary propositional deductions) include the left lateral prefrontal cortex and the left inferior parietal lobule; (2) Activity in these regions is present at the time of inference and is greater the longer the time needed for drawing the conclusion.

(1) the generation of conclusions in propositional deductions is accompanied by activity in a left-lateralized network that consists of frontal (BA 6, BA 44) and parietal (BA 40) areas and (2) the activity is greater for the longer the reasoning times.
the generation of conclusions in propositional deduction is associated with increased activity in a network that consists of the left inferior frontal gyrus and the left supramarginal gyrus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural correlates of elementary deductive reasoning.
the neural basis of the generation of conclusions in everyday life, elementary propositional deductions, and with the neural correlates of the different types of deductive inferences.
the neural basis of the generation of inferences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural basis of elementary deduction is a left lateralized network, including Brodmann Areas 44, 6, and 40.
the neural basis of elementary deduction involves a network of left lateralized brain regions, including the inferior frontal gyrus and the inferior parietal labe.

the neural basis for elementary propositional deduction is located in the left frontal and parietal lobes, and that the frontal areas seem to be more involved in the generation of conclusions than in their verification.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the brain regions implicated in elementary deductions are different from those implicated in other types of deductively valid inferences, including those based on syllogistic forms of reasoning, which are known to be more complex.

the brain areas implicated in elementary propositional deduction are the same areas implicated in the processing of linguistic material, and that the areas implicated in the generation of conclusions in this type of deduction are the same as the areas implicated in working memory.
the neural basis of reasoning is a complex system of brain areas, including frontal, temporal and parietal lobes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a single entity, and different brain regions may have specific functions in different types of reasoning.
the brain regions implicated in elementary deductive reasoning can be reliably identified by using multiple and independent criteria derived from the two leading theories in the field.

it provides a first step toward the identification of brain regions specifically associated with the drawing of elementary deductive inferences, and it provides a first glimpse of a neural network for elementary deductive reasoning in the human brain.
